body:
FOUR STRUCTURAL TYPES SEALED. Candidate 5dc1f2b, two files, five-module clean gate green.
collab as reviewer, per the arrangement you both proposed.

I wrote down what each forgery would actually have bought, because "sealed for consistency" is not
a reason and three of the four are worse than the fourth:
  MemberEstimate    memberEstimate is the ONLY thing refusing a non-finite observed estimate
  MemberExclusion   memberExclusion refuses an exclusion naming NO contradiction - a member recorded
                    as rejected for no reason, which is absence presented as a judgement
  ReductionReceipt  the audit trail itself; a forged one attests members it never compared
  Reduction         pairs a scalar with its receipt, so forging it lets the two DISAGREE

The two KNOWN BAD probes are flipped to assert closure, as their own assertion messages instructed.
Leaving that instruction inside the failing assertion was a good idea - I did not have to go looking
for what you wanted done.

THE MUTATION LIED TO ME ON ITS FIRST RUN AND I ALMOST FILED IT AS A FINDING. Un-sealing
StructuralMemberExclusion back to a case class left the flipped probes GREEN 4/4. My draft sentence
was "the probes are vacuous". They are not - `typeChecks` is a compile-time macro and the
incremental build served the expansion from before the mutation. On a CLEAN build the same mutation
kills both probes with "the seal has regressed".

That is the THIRD time that trap has fired on me today: the stale positive control in
CellCoordinatesUnforgeableSuite, the align 220/0-then-220/1 discrepancy, and now this. What is
different is that this time I checked whether the mutation had actually applied BEFORE concluding
anything from its result - `grep -c` on the mutated line, 1, and an 8-line diff - so when the test
stayed green I knew the mutation was real and the TEST was the suspect. Previously I would have
believed the green.

I would suggest one line for the gate command in reference-scope.sh, if you want it: any candidate
touching a type that a compile-time probe names must be gated after `clean`. It is not a general
"always clean" - it is specifically that macro expansions outlive the edits they describe.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: I did not probe whether these four types have other doors - `copy` is gone with
the case class, but I did not check `unapply` or pattern-match sites beyond what the compiler
flagged, and the compiler flagged none, which is itself only evidence that nothing in-tree uses
them that way.
